title: LiDAR vs Ultrasonic
description: Same basic trick, same room — but each one fails in a completely different place. Knowing where is half of choosing well.

content.value: You've now met both time-of-flight sensors this course covers. Neither one is simply "better" — each is a genuine trade-off, and the right choice depends entirely on the room and the budget.

ULTRASONIC              LiDAR
price               ~₹100                    ~₹2,000+
coverage             one direction            full 360°
resolution           coarse                   fine, degree-by-degree
range                a few metres              tens of metres
fails on glass       no — sound passes through glass poorly, but doesn't
                      get fooled by transparency the way light does
fails on soft/angled  yes — soft fabric absorbs sound, angled            
 surfaces              surfaces deflect the echo

Glass is nearly invisible to LiDAR: light passes straight through it instead of reflecting back, so a glass door can register as open space that isn't actually there. Sound behaves differently against glass, which is one of the reasons the two sensors are sometimes used together rather than as strict alternatives — each one's blind spot is the other's strength.
A thick curtain or a soft couch cushion absorbs sound far more readily than it absorbs light, so ultrasonic can miss or badly under-read soft furnishings that LiDAR sees clearly.

Notice both of these are the same lesson from Module 7's ultrasonic angle problem, generalised: every distance sensor has physical situations where its measuring trick simply breaks down. Knowing your sensor's specific failure modes matters as much as knowing how it works.

Key takeaway: ultrasonic is cheap and single-direction; LiDAR is expensive but gives a full, fine-resolution map. Each has real physical blind spots — glass for LiDAR, soft or angled surfaces for ultrasonic — and a well-designed robot often needs to know both.

quiz.question: Why might a glass door confuse a LiDAR sensor but not necessarily an ultrasonic one?
options: Light passes through glass rather than reflecting, so LiDAR can read "open space" where there's actually a door
LiDAR can't detect anything transparent, ever, including walls
Glass doesn't exist as a real material to sensors
quiz.explain: Transparency to light is exactly the failure mode — the laser doesn't bounce back the way it would off a solid, opaque wall.

quiz.question: Why does a thick curtain sometimes fool an ultrasonic sensor?
options: Curtains reflect sound perfectly, giving a false near reading
Soft fabric absorbs sound rather than reflecting it cleanly, so little or no echo returns
Ultrasonic sensors can't detect fabric of any kind
quiz.explain: Soft, absorbent materials swallow the sound pulse instead of bouncing it back — the same underlying issue as the angled-wall problem from Module 7, just a different cause.

quiz.question: Why would a real robot sometimes use both sensor types rather than picking just one?
options: Each sensor's blind spot (glass for LiDAR, soft/angled surfaces for ultrasonic) is different, so combining them covers more real-world situations
Using two sensors always doubles accuracy with no downside
quiz.explain: Since their failure modes don't overlap, pairing them lets one catch what the other misses — a common real engineering trade-off.
